issues.legal_issue: A statutory officer cannot review a final order when the governing law does not confer review power, and a final order cannot be reopened through a restoration application outside the prescribed remedies.
material_facts: The competent officer issued notices to the non-evacuee co-sharers, but no claim was filed, and an order vesting the evacuee interest in the Custodian was made.
The co-sharers did not appeal or seek revision of that order, which became final under the governing law.

The co-sharers later obtained orders setting aside the vesting order and transferring the evacuee interest to them through a restoration application; the officer subsequently reviewed those orders after applications by the Assistant Custodian.
The governing law provided for appeal and revision but contained no provision authorizing the competent officer to review his own orders.
issues.conclusion: Review is a creature of statute and cannot be exercised without statutory authority. The orders reopening the final vesting order and the later review orders were without jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: The Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951, sections 6, 7, 11, 14 and 15 provided for notices, claims, vesting, appeal and revision; section 18 made orders final subject to the Act’s express exceptions. The Court applied the principle that review is available only where statute provides for it, relying on Harbhajan Singh v. Karam Singh, which approved Baijnath Ram Goenka v. Nand Kumar Singh and Anantharaju Shetty v. Appu Hegde, and reiterated Patel Chunibhai Dajibhai v. Narayanrao Khanderao Jambekar.

predicates.statutory_officer_order_review_proceedin: A proceeding seeks reconsideration by a statutory officer of an order the officer previously made.
predicates.review_power_not_conferred: The governing legal scheme does not authorize that officer to review the order.

issues.definition: When a proceeding seeks review of a statutory officer’s order and the governing legal scheme grants no review power, the review order is without authority.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s conduct can disentitle it to discretionary constitutional writ relief even when the challenged administrative order is itself without jurisdiction.
material_facts: The co-sharers received individual notices but filed no claims and did not appeal or seek revision of the vesting order.
After the order had become final, they sought restoration and obtained orders in their favour by invoking a review power that did not exist.
The Assistant Custodian later invoked the same review jurisdiction on grounds adverse to the co-sharers, who then challenged the resulting orders by writ petition.
The co-sharers had used the unauthorized review process for their own advantage, to the detriment of the allottee.
issues.conclusion: The co-sharers’ conduct disentitled them to certiorari, and the High Court should have dismissed their writ petition. The absence of jurisdiction was not cured by waiver, but it did not require the Court to grant writ relief to parties whose conduct disentitled them to it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court exercises extraordinary, discretionary jurisdiction and may consider the conduct of the party seeking relief. Although waiver cannot cure a want of jurisdiction, that does not oblige a court to grant a writ to a party whose conduct disentitles it to relief. The statutory finality and appeal and revision framework in sections 14, 15 and 18 of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951, informed the significance of the co-sharers’ failure to use the available remedies.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A party seeks constitutional writ relief against an administrative order.
predicates.party_previously_used_unauthorized_revie: The party earlier invoked a review process that was not authorized and obtained a benefit through it.
predicates.party_had_notice_and_did_not_use_availab: The party had notice of the original order but did not pursue the available appeal or revision remedies.

issues.definition: When a party seeks constitutional writ relief after benefiting from unauthorized review, and had notice of the original order but did not use available remedies, the party is disentitled to discretionary writ relief.
